candidates.current_role: Texas Attorney General since 2015; Republican nominee for U.S. Senate
candidates.background: Ken Paxton is a lawyer who has served as Texas Attorney General since January 2015. He previously represented the McKinney area in the Texas House (District 70, 2003 to 2013) and the Texas Senate (District 8, 2013 to 2015). He holds degrees from Baylor University and the University of Virginia School of Law. He won the Republican nomination by defeating Sen. John Cornyn in the May 26, 2026 runoff with about 64 percent of the vote.

priorities.text: Says his top priorities are lowering costs, restoring the American Dream and keeping Texas safe.
Campaigns on helping President Trump finish the border wall and deport people in the country illegally.
Campaigns on income tax deductions for health care costs, home purchases and healthy living, and on doubling the child tax credit.
Campaigns on taking on what he calls Big Pharma and Big Food and increasing transparency in the food and health care industries.
Says he will defend gun rights and "defend the unborn."
Campaigns on keeping the United States ahead of China in artificial intelligence while protecting Texas communities, land and children.

promises.text: Proposes a $25,000 deduction for out-of-pocket medical expenses including premiums (plus $25,000 per dependent), a $5,000 healthy-lifestyle deduction, and $50,000 deductions for first-time homebuyers and for down payments on a new primary residence.
Proposes doubling the maximum child tax credit from $2,200 to $4,400 and making the "Trump accounts" program permanent.
Says he would ban Chinese technology from U.S. data centers and hold companies criminally liable if their data centers power AI chatbots that endanger children.
Supports permanent repeal of the federal gas tax.

record.text: As attorney general, led the multistate legal challenge seeking to strike down the Affordable Care Act, which the U.S. Supreme Court dismissed in June 2021.
Filed Texas v. Pennsylvania at the U.S. Supreme Court challenging the 2020 presidential election results in four states; the case was unsuccessful.
As attorney general, sued the Biden administration over immigration policies including a deportation pause and parole-in-place, and led litigation to end the DACA program.
Defended the state's Rio Grande buoy barrier in federal court; the full Fifth Circuit allowed the buoys to remain while the case continued (2024).
Sued Austin, San Marcos, Killeen, Elgin and Denton in January 2024 to overturn voter-approved ordinances that limited enforcement of low-level marijuana possession laws.
Sued doctors in 2024 under SB 14, the 2023 law barring gender transition treatments for minors, seeking penalties and license revocation.
Sued the EPA in March 2024 over its oil and gas methane emissions rule, and joined a 22-state suit in January 2025 against the federal methane emissions fee.
Sued out-of-state and foreign providers accused of mailing abortion pills to Texans and defended the state's abortion ban in court.
Authored anti-abortion legislation beginning in 2003 as a member of the Texas House.
Pledged in 2025 to defend the state's new education savings account (school choice) law in court.
Proposed rules in 2026 to implement SB 17, the 2025 law restricting land purchases by entities tied to China, Russia, Iran and North Korea.

notes.text: The Texas House impeached Paxton in May 2023 on 20 articles (vote 121-23), alleging misuse of office to help donor Nate Paul; the Texas Senate acquitted him on all articles in September 2023 and he returned to office.

Paxton was indicted in 2015 on state securities fraud charges. In March 2024 he entered a pretrial agreement requiring community service, legal ethics courses and about $271,000 in restitution, with the charges to be dropped; he denied wrongdoing.

In April 2025 a Travis County judge awarded $6.6 million to four former deputies who said they were fired after reporting Paxton to the FBI; Paxton dropped his appeal in July 2025 and the state will pay the judgment.
The Texas Tribune reported that the Wall Street Journal found his blind trust trustee sent him a 2020 list of $618,000 in stock purchases, which experts said may have violated trust rules.
Paxton did not respond to the Texas Tribune's 2026 primary or general election questionnaires; the Tribune compiled his positions from past statements.
As of Oct. 8, 2026, no Paxton-Talarico debate had been scheduled; Paxton had declined or not responded to invitations.
He received an endorsement from the largest union for Border Patrol agents.

q_tariffs.summary: Told the Houston Chronicle in April 2025 that he fully supports President Trump's tariff actions; he has not answered questions on specific current tariffs.

q_federal_spending.summary: Calls himself a fiscal conservative who would stop wasteful spending and praised the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act as historic legislation.

q_vouchers.summary: As attorney general, celebrated the 2025 Texas school choice law as a win for parents and vowed to defend it in court.

q_medicaid.summary: Led the legal effort to strike down the Affordable Care Act, the law that created Medicaid expansion; no direct statement on expanding Medicaid in Texas was found.

q_abortion.summary: Has defended the state's near-total abortion ban in court, sued providers who mail abortion pills to Texans, and says he will "defend the unborn" in the Senate.

q_border_state.summary: As attorney general, defended state border measures such as the Rio Grande buoy barrier in court and says "we need a secure border."

q_deportation.summary: Lists deporting people in the country illegally among the Trump priorities he would champion in the Senate.

q_legal_status.summary: Led lawsuits to end DACA and to stop parole-in-place for undocumented spouses of citizens.

q_gun_laws.summary: Condemned the 2022 Bipartisan Safer Communities Act, which included red flag incentives and expanded background checks for young buyers, as infringing on Second Amendment rights.

q_cannabis.summary: Sued cities to block marijuana decriminalization ordinances; when asked about Texas THC restrictions in August 2026, said "I don't know the details of it."

q_fossil_priority.summary: Sued asset managers over efforts to move away from coal and opposed federal climate rules he said would harm the oil and gas industry.

q_oilgas_rules.summary: Sued to block the federal oil and gas methane rule and the federal methane emissions fee.

q_foreign_land.summary: Praised SB 17 for preventing the Chinese government from buying Texas farmland, property, minerals and water rights, and cited a Chinese billionaire's land purchase near Laughlin Air Force Base as a security concern.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports the SAVE America Act requiring proof of citizenship to register and photo ID at the polls, and offered to consider leaving the race if senators ended the filibuster to pass it.

q_trans_minors.summary: Has sued doctors under the state ban on gender transition treatments for minors and issued an opinion extending the ban to mental health providers.

issue_notes.summary: Supports President Trump's military campaign against Iran, saying Iran cannot be allowed to become nuclear, while saying he would seek more intelligence before deciding on war powers votes.

Supports requiring data centers to pay their own infrastructure costs, more efficient water systems, ending state sales tax breaks and keeping them away from homes, and backs the DATA Act allowing off-grid power.
Favors tax deductions for out-of-pocket medical costs and premiums rather than expanded government programs.
Called the plan for border barrier construction in Big Bend National Park "not smart border security" and welcomed the August 2026 pause, without taking a firm stance on construction inside the park.
Supports a pro-growth regulatory framework for cryptocurrency, including passage of the CLARITY Act.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 50 (North Austin); Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate
candidates.background: James Talarico is a former sixth-grade teacher from Round Rock who has served in the Texas House since 2019, first for District 52 and since 2023 for District 50. He holds degrees from the University of Texas at Austin, the Harvard Graduate School of Education and Austin Presbyterian Theological Seminary. He worked for the nonprofit Reasoning Mind before running for office. He won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary over Jasmine Crockett with 52.4 percent.

priorities.text: Campaigns on reducing the influence of money in politics, including banning corporate PACs and super PACs.
Campaigns on a "New American Dream" economic agenda to lower costs and raise pay, framing politics as "top versus bottom."
Campaigns on higher taxes on billionaires and corporations paired with a middle-class "cost-of-living tax cut."
Campaigns on lowering health care costs through a Medicare buy-in for all ages and caps on drug costs.
Campaigns on tighter regulation of data centers so they pay for their own energy infrastructure.
Campaigns on ending what he calls forever wars in the Middle East.

promises.text: Says he will push to raise the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour and expand overtime eligibility.
Says he will work to allow every American to join Medicare and to restore enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits.
Says he will vote for a war powers resolution to end the war with Iran.
Says he will work to repeal President Trump's tariffs.
Says he will seek to ban members of Congress from trading individual stocks.
Says he would suspend the federal gas tax.

record.text: Helped pass the 2021 law capping insulin copays at $25 a month.
Coauthored HB 3, the 2019 school finance law.
Voted against SB 2, the 2025 education savings account (voucher) bill, and says he led House opposition to it.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), the ban on gender transition treatments for minors, and for all 18 proposed Democratic amendments to it.
Voted against SB 8 (2021), the six-week abortion ban, and against HB 1927 (2021), permitless carry.
Voted against SB 4 (2023), which made illegal entry a state crime, and against SB 8 (2025), which requires many sheriffs to sign agreements with ICE.
Voted against SB 10 (2025), the Ten Commandments classroom display law, and SB 17 (2025), the foreign land purchase restrictions.
Voted for HB 441 (2021) and HB 218 (2023), which reduced penalties for low-level marijuana possession, and against SB 3 (2025), the THC product ban.
Voted for SB 2627 (2023), the electric generation funding bill, and for the House version of the 2023 and 2025 state budgets.
Recorded as voting no on SB 9 (2025), the bail bill, but filed a statement saying he intended to vote yes; voted for SJR 5 (2025), the bail constitutional amendment.
Joined Democratic quorum breaks in 2021 over the election bill and in 2025 over mid-decade congressional redistricting; voted against SB 1 (2021) and HB 4 (2025).

notes.text: Attorney General Ken Paxton sought to remove Talarico and 12 other House Democrats from office over the 2025 quorum break; the Texas Supreme Court dismissed the case for lack of jurisdiction in May 2026.
PolitiFact rated False a September 2026 Texas PAC ad claiming Talarico supported taxpayer-funded gender surgeries for young children.
Talarico accepted televised debate invitations and proposed a Fox News debate; as of Oct. 8, 2026 no debate with Paxton had been scheduled.
He says he has not taken corporate PAC money since his first race in 2017.

q_tariffs.summary: Calls for repealing President Trump's tariffs, saying they raise costs and cost jobs, including tariffs on farm inputs.

q_federal_spending.summary: Opposes federal cuts to Medicaid, Medicare, SNAP and WIC and would reverse recent Medicaid cuts; proposes reducing the deficit partly through higher taxes on the wealthy and ending wars.

q_min_wage.summary: Supports raising the federal minimum wage to $15 an hour.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against the 2025 Texas voucher program and opposes national voucher efforts.

q_medicaid.summary: Has pushed for Texas to accept Medicaid expansion and supports letting every American join Medicare.

q_abortion.summary: Supports federal legislation to codify Roe v. Wade and has voted against abortion restrictions in the Legislature.

q_deportation.summary: Says ICE should focus on criminals, gang members and human traffickers rather than law-abiding taxpayers, and supports more Border Patrol agents.

q_legal_status.summary: Supports a path to citizenship for long-term immigrants, spouses and DREAMers, and backs the Dignity Act framework.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports universal background checks, safe storage requirements and a higher purchase age for certain semi-automatic rifles.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports legalizing and regulating marijuana for adults, authored a state bill to do so, and opposed the Texas THC ban.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Favors an all-of-the-above approach that restores renewable energy tax credits while partnering with oil and gas; voted for the 2023 state electric generation funding bill.

q_oilgas_rules.summary: Supports finishing the job of plugging abandoned oil and gas wells and strengthening the Clean Air Act, while streamlining energy permitting.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025), which restricts land purchases by people and entities tied to certain foreign adversaries.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act and broke quorum in 2021 over the state election bill.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against the 2023 state ban, citing its breadth, but in 2026 said he opposes gender reassignment surgery for minors and favors a national ban on such surgery.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025) and called a 2023 version "un-constitutional" and "deeply un-Christian."

issue_notes.summary: Calls for ending the war with Iran and says money spent on Middle East wars should be spent at home.
Says data centers raise utility bills and should pay for their own infrastructure; supports local authority over data centers and federal AI safety rules.
Supports term limits and a binding ethics code for justices.
Says he would stop the border wall project through Big Bend National Park while supporting barriers where needed.
Opposes warrantless use of license plate reader data, saying constant warrantless surveillance has no place in a free society.
Proposes banning Wall Street firms from buying up housing stock, expanding the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit and down payment help for first-time buyers.

candidates.current_role: Retired insurance adjuster; Libertarian nominee for U.S. Senate
candidates.background: Ted Brown is a retired independent insurance adjuster who lives in the Wells Branch area of Austin. He earned a political science degree from UCLA in 1984. He is a former chair of the Libertarian Party of California and is vice chair of the Libertarian Party of Travis County. He was the Libertarian nominee for U.S. Senate in 2024, receiving more than 267,000 votes.

priorities.text: Campaigns on limited government, personal freedom, economic freedom and a non-interventionist foreign policy.
Campaigns on repealing the federal income tax and abolishing the IRS, paired with large spending cuts.
Campaigns on digital privacy, opposing age verification laws, digital ID and government surveillance.
Campaigns on ending the war on drugs and legalizing marijuana.
Campaigns on free trade and ending President Trump's tariffs.

promises.text: Says he will never vote to raise taxes.
Says he would introduce a bill requiring congressional approval of every executive order and emergency declaration before it takes effect.
Says he will vote against red flag laws and work to repeal existing gun control laws.
Says he would support every war powers resolution and vote against appropriations for foreign deployments.

notes.text: Brown rejects the spoiler label and says a vote for a third-party candidate is not wasted.
A Texas Southern University poll reported by FOX 7 showed Brown at about 3 percent.

q_tariffs.summary: Says tariffs are taxes on consumers that invite retaliation, and would eliminate every tariff change President Trump has made.

q_federal_spending.summary: Calls for massive federal spending cuts and across-the-board budget cuts to address the national debt.

q_vouchers.summary: Prefers tuition tax credits over vouchers, saying vouchers could lead to government control of private schools, and would abolish the federal Department of Education.

q_medicaid.summary: Calls health care a service best provided by the free market and lists Medicare and Medicaid among causes of rising health costs.

q_border_state.summary: Opposes Operation Lone Star, saying immigration is a federal issue, and opposes further border wall construction.

q_deportation.summary: Calls for abolishing ICE, ending raids and forced deportations, and closing detention facilities.

q_legal_status.summary: Supports an Ellis Island-style system with free movement of people and work authorization from day one, which would allow peaceful immigrants to stay legally.

q_gun_laws.summary: Would repeal existing gun control laws and vote against red flag laws.

q_cannabis.summary: Would remove marijuana from the controlled substances schedule, repeal federal drug laws and end state cannabis prohibitions.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Supports an energy market including oil, gas, wind and solar without subsidies, and supports more nuclear power plants.

q_trans_minors.summary: Says the federal government should have no authority over the doctor-patient relationship, while saying he is not advocating surgery for minors.

issue_notes.summary: Opposes Flock and other public surveillance cameras, would bar federal funds for license plate readers and require warrants for police data requests.
Would abolish civil asset forfeiture, end mandatory minimum sentences and end qualified immunity for police; opposes the death penalty.
Would bring all troops home, withdraw from NATO and end foreign aid; opposes the war with Iran.
Favors medical savings accounts, tax-deductible health expenses, buying insurance across state lines and buying drugs from other countries.
Would repeal the federal gas tax completely.

candidates.background: Greg Abbott has been governor since January 2015 and is seeking a fourth term. He previously served as Texas Attorney General (2002 to 2015), as a justice on the Texas Supreme Court (1996 to 2001) and as a state district judge in Houston. He holds degrees from the University of Texas at Austin and Vanderbilt University law school. He won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 81.8 percent.

priorities.text: Campaigns on cutting property taxes, including letting voters decide whether to eliminate school district property taxes on homeowners.
Campaigns on lowering housing, energy, health care and insurance costs through his "Keep Texas Affordable" plan.
Campaigns on public safety, including bail restrictions, a statewide prosecutor and impeachment of district attorneys he says fail to enforce the law.
Campaigns on border security and cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.
Campaigns on school choice and directing more education dollars to classrooms.

promises.text: Proposes limiting local government spending growth to population plus inflation or 3.5 percent, whichever is lower.
Proposes requiring two-thirds voter approval for all local property tax increases and allowing rollback elections when 15 percent of voters petition.
Proposes appraising property once every five years and lowering the homestead appraisal cap from 10 percent to 3 percent, extending it to all property.
Proposes automatically denying bail to people in the country illegally who are charged with a felony.
Proposes requiring 70 percent of school funding to go to classrooms, audits of district spending, and limits on classroom screen time.
Proposes opening Austin and San Antonio municipal utilities to retail electric competition and capping monthly copays for inhalers and epinephrine at $25.
Proposes a $400 million roof fortification program offering up to $10,000 per homeowner.

record.text: Signed SB 2 (2025), creating the state's education savings account (voucher) program.
Signed HB 2 (2025), the school finance law that lawmakers approved with about $8.5 billion in new funding, mostly for teacher pay.
Signed the Texas Heartbeat Act (2021), banning most abortions after about six weeks.
Signed permitless carry legislation in June 2021; after the 2018 Santa Fe shooting he said a red flag law was not necessary in Texas.
Launched Operation Lone Star in 2021, deploying state troopers and National Guard soldiers to the border and starting construction of a state border wall.
Signed SB 4 (2023), making illegal entry a state crime, and SB 8 (2025), requiring many sheriffs to enter agreements with ICE.
Signed SB 1 (2021), the election law described in its caption as preventing fraud and increasing criminal penalties.
Signed SB 14 (2023), barring gender transition procedures for minors, and in 2022 directed state agencies to treat such treatments for minors as child abuse.
Signed SB 10 (2025), requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in public school classrooms, and SB 17 (2025), restricting land purchases by certain foreign entities.
Vetoed SB 3 (2025), which would have banned hemp-derived THC products, and in September 2025 ordered state agencies to bar sales to people under 21.
Signed HB 2127 (2023), which limits city and county ordinances in several policy areas.
Signed SB 9 (2025), the bail reform law, and SB 7 (2025), on financing of water infrastructure.
Signed the 2025 mid-decade congressional map, saying it ensures fairer representation.
In August 2026 ordered state agencies to stop spending state money on Flock license plate reader cameras, citing privacy.
In 2020 limited each county to one mail ballot drop-off location, citing illegal voting.

notes.text: Abbott had about $96 million in campaign funds at the end of February 2026, compared with about $617,000 for Gina Hinojosa.
Abbott did not accept debate invitations that Hinojosa accepted, according to the Hinojosa campaign; the Texas Tribune reported he has largely ignored her on the campaign trail.

Emails released in 2019 showed Abbott drove a 2018 review that flagged nearly 100,000 registered voters; the review was canceled after officials acknowledged many naturalized citizens were wrongly flagged.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Proposes a constitutional amendment letting voters eliminate school district property taxes on homeowners, paid for with budget surpluses.

q_spending_cap.summary: Proposes limiting local government spending growth to population plus inflation or 3.5 percent, whichever is lower.

q_vouchers.summary: Led passage of and signed the 2025 education savings account program.

q_school_funding.summary: Signed the 2025 school finance law with about $8.5 billion mostly for teacher pay, and now emphasizes directing funds to classrooms and auditing administrative costs.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Signed SB 10 (2025) requiring classroom displays of the Ten Commandments.

q_medicaid.summary: Has long opposed Medicaid expansion, calling it "wrong for Texas"; supported extending postpartum coverage to 12 months.

q_abortion.summary: Signed the six-week abortion ban and supports the current law, which has no exceptions for rape or incest.

q_border_state.summary: Launched and continues Operation Lone Star, the state border security effort that has cost more than $11 billion.

q_deportation.summary: Signed SB 8 (2025) requiring sheriff agreements with ICE and says the state is working with the federal government to detain and deport undocumented immigrants.

q_gun_laws.summary: Signed permitless carry in 2021 and has said a red flag law is not necessary in Texas.

q_bail.summary: Signed the 2025 bail package he calls the toughest in state history and proposes automatic bail denial for people in the country illegally charged with felonies.

q_cannabis.summary: Vetoed the 2025 THC ban and favored regulation with an age limit of 21, but in 2019 told cities to keep enforcing marijuana laws.

q_foreign_land.summary: Signed SB 17 (2025) restricting land purchases by certain foreign entities.

q_water.summary: Signed SB 7 (2025) on the oversight and financing of water infrastructure.

q_voting_access.summary: Signed SB 1 (2021), which added voting rules and criminal penalties, and limited mail ballot drop-off sites in 2020.

q_election_fraud.summary: Signed SB 1 (2021), which its caption describes as preventing fraud and increasing criminal penalties.

q_preemption.summary: Signed HB 2127 (2023) limiting local ordinances and proposes barring cities from housing rules he says undermine state law, withholding sales tax from cities that do not comply.

q_trans_minors.summary: Signed SB 14 (2023) barring gender transition procedures for minors.

issue_notes.summary: Ordered state agencies to stop funding Flock cameras and said they must be used responsibly if used at all.
His campaign rejected calls to suspend the state gas tax, saying it would take money from roads and schools without easing prices.
Signed the 2025 mid-decade congressional map drawn to add Republican seats.
His campaign says new data centers are being paused and must pay their own way, provide their own power and reuse their own water.
Proposes an Essential Benefits Health Insurance Plan exempt from some state mandates, which he says could cut premiums by nearly 20 percent.
Proposes tuition discounts for summer courses and three-year bachelor's degree options at public universities.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 49 (Austin), since 2017; Democratic nominee for governor
candidates.background: Gina Hinojosa is a civil rights and labor lawyer who grew up in Brownsville and has represented central Austin in the Texas House since 2017. She served on the Austin ISD board of trustees from 2012 to 2016, including as board president. She holds degrees from the University of Texas at Austin and George Washington University Law School. She won the March 3, 2026 Democratic primary for governor.

priorities.text: Campaigns on saving Texas public schools, including ending the STAAR test and the voucher program.
Campaigns on putting money in Texans' pockets through a one-time $1,500 refund to every household from the Rainy Day Fund.
Campaigns on ending what she calls the "Greg Abbott Corruption Tax."
Campaigns on an immediate moratorium on new data centers.
Campaigns on expanding health care access, including Medicaid expansion and strengthening rural hospitals.

promises.text: Says she will name the affordability crisis an emergency item on her first day so lawmakers can pass the $1,500 refund.
Says that on day one she will fire Education Commissioner Mike Morath and appoint an educator to lead the Texas Education Agency.
Says she will end the STAAR test, pause A-F school ratings and return taken-over school districts to their communities.
Says she will audit and terminate education vendor contracts and redirect the money to make teachers among the highest paid in the nation.
Says she will direct the Public Utility Commission to freeze residential electricity rates until data centers and other large users are required to cover their own costs.
Pledged to veto any partisan gerrymandered maps.

record.text: Voted against SB 2 (2025), the education savings account program, and helped lead House opposition to it.
Voted for HB 2 (2025), the school finance bill; was a negotiator of the 2019 school finance law.
Voted against SB 8 (2021), the six-week abortion ban, and HB 1927 (2021), permitless carry.
Voted against SB 14 (2023), the ban on gender transition treatments for minors, and SB 10 (2025), the Ten Commandments display law.
Voted against SB 4 (2023) and SB 8 (2025), the state immigration enforcement laws, and SB 17 (2025), the foreign land purchase restrictions.
Voted for HB 441 (2021) and HB 218 (2023), reducing penalties for low-level marijuana possession, and against SB 3 (2025), the THC ban.
Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the bail constitutional amendment, and HJR 7 (2025), the dedicated water fund amendment; was recorded absent on SB 9 (2025).
Voted against HB 2127 (2023), the state preemption law, and HB 1243 (2023), which increased the penalty for illegal voting.
Voted against SB 2627 (2023), the electric generation funding bill, and against the House versions of the 2023 and 2025 state budgets.
Joined Democratic quorum breaks in 2021 over the election bill and in 2025 over congressional redistricting; voted against HB 4 (2025), the new congressional map.
Authored a 2025 bill to stop institutional investors from buying more than 10 single-family homes.

notes.text: The Texas Supreme Court in May 2026 dismissed the attorney general's case seeking removal of House Democrats who broke quorum in 2025.
Hinojosa accepted televised debate invitations, including an October 15 forum; the campaign says Abbott did not respond.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Proposes ending corporate subsidies and using the savings to cut property taxes, with the end goal of eliminating residential property taxes.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against the 2025 voucher program, calls it a payout for the privileged and wants to end it.

q_school_funding.summary: Wants Texas teachers to be among the highest paid in the nation and authored the Fully Fund Our Future Act in 2023.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025), which requires classroom displays.

q_medicaid.summary: Calls Medicaid expansion a central part of her plan to lower health costs and cover every Texas child.

q_abortion.summary: Supports restoring legal abortion access, including for rape, incest and fatal fetal diagnoses, and voted against the 2021 ban.

q_border_state.summary: Says the state's border spending is wasteful when crossings are at record lows and criticizes no-bid Operation Lone Star contracts.

q_deportation.summary: Says migrants who contribute to their communities should not be rounded up or deported, calls for closing the Dilley family detention center, and voted against SB 8 (2025).

q_gun_laws.summary: Voted against the 2021 permitless carry law.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SJR 5 (2025), the constitutional amendment requiring denial of bail in certain felony cases.

q_cannabis.summary: Voted for bills reducing penalties for marijuana possession in 2021 and 2023 and against the 2025 THC ban.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Voted against SB 2627 (2023), which created funding mechanisms for new electric generating facilities.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025) restricting land purchases by certain foreign entities.

q_water.summary: Voted for HJR 7 (2025), dedicating sales tax revenue to the Texas water fund.

q_voting_access.summary: Joined the 2021 quorum break against the state election bill.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted against HB 1243 (2023), which increased the criminal penalty for illegal voting.

q_preemption.summary: Voted against HB 2127 (2023), which limits local ordinances.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), the state ban on gender transition treatments for minors.

issue_notes.summary: Says Flock cameras have become a tool for warrantless surveillance and should be taken down statewide.
Called on Abbott to suspend the state gas tax and backfill road and school funding from the surplus or Rainy Day Fund.
Supports nonpartisan redistricting and pledges to veto maps gerrymandered to benefit either party.
Proposes stopping private equity firms from buying up single-family homes and holding landlords accountable for AI-driven rent pricing.
Wants an executive order for an immediate data center moratorium and a special session to repeal data center tax breaks.

candidates.current_role: Engineer and business owner; Libertarian nominee for governor
candidates.background: Pat Dixon is a process control engineer and president of DPAS Inc. who has worked for companies including Honeywell and Emerson. He holds an engineering degree from Miami University in Ohio. He served on the Lago Vista City Council from 2005 to 2009 and chaired the Libertarian Party of Texas for 10 years. He has previously run for the Texas Senate and Travis County commissioner.

priorities.text: Campaigns on "right sizing government," meaning people can do what they want as long as they do not harm others.
Campaigns on identifying specific state and local spending cuts before promising tax relief.
Campaigns on ending corporate welfare, including tax incentives for AI data centers.
Campaigns on parent and teacher empowerment, including a statewide scholarship that follows each child to any school.
Campaigns on election reforms including approval voting and nonpartisan redistricting.

promises.text: Says that as governor he would refuse to take part in immigration enforcement that harms the life, liberty and property of Texans.
Says that as governor he would decline a presidential request to redraw districts in the president's favor.

record.text: Served two terms on the Lago Vista City Council (2005 to 2009), where he says he worked to reduce spending.

notes.text: Former U.S. Rep. Ron Paul endorsed Dixon for governor in October 2026.
Dixon answered the League of Women Voters (VOTE411) and iVoterGuide questionnaires and posted his responses.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Is skeptical of promises to eliminate property taxes without detailed spending cuts and cautions against replacing them with sales taxes.

q_min_wage.summary: Opposes the minimum wage, citing Milton Friedman.

q_vouchers.summary: Ideally wants a statewide scholarship giving every child the same amount to follow them to any school, and opposes turning away voucher applicants.

q_abortion.summary: Calls himself pro-life but says he will not impose his religion as governor and that doctors and adults should make difficult medical decisions; disagrees with enforcing the Comstock Act.

q_border_state.summary: Says the governor does not make federal border policy and Texas can cooperate with enforcement, but would refuse cooperation that harms Texans' rights.

q_deportation.summary: Says "if you are peaceful and productive, welcome" and does not support the current means ICE uses to enforce immigration law.

q_legal_status.summary: Says his federal policy would be to welcome peaceful and productive immigrants and that legal immigration is nearly impossible under current law.

q_gun_laws.summary: Defends lawful gun uses, raises due process concerns about red flag laws and opposes broad mental health screening of gun owners.

q_cannabis.summary: Says adults should be free to make their own choices, applauded Abbott's veto of the THC ban and says Texas should go further.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Considers nuclear the best long-term option but prefers that market forces drive energy choices.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports voter verification but says photo ID burdens some eligible voters and suggests biometrics on voter registration cards.

q_preemption.summary: Says he will respect local control.

q_gambling.summary: Agrees with expanding gambling, saying prohibitions are unenforceable.

q_trans_minors.summary: Was neutral, saying he would be reluctant to intervene when parents and child consent under professional supervision but opposes transition without parental consent.

issue_notes.summary: Opposes taxpayer incentives for data centers and says growth should pay for itself, but would not oppose centers that pay for their impact.
Says Texas elections are conducted properly and results are legitimate; supports approval voting and nonpartisan redistricting.
Says opening the market to new competitors and lower-cost providers will lower prices.

candidates.background: Dan Patrick has been lieutenant governor, the presiding officer of the Texas Senate, since January 2015. He previously represented Houston-area Senate District 7 from 2007 to 2015. Before office he was a television sportscaster, conservative talk radio host and radio station owner. He holds a bachelor's degree in English from the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, and won the March 3, 2026 Republican primary with 84.7 percent.

priorities.text: Campaigns on lowering property and business taxes, including larger homestead exemptions.
Campaigns on strengthening the electric grid by adding reliable thermal power.
Campaigns on school choice and what he calls a high-quality education for all.
Campaigns on securing the border and supporting law enforcement.
Campaigns on protecting life, religious freedom and the Second Amendment.

record.text: Designated school choice (SB 2), a THC ban (SB 3), a $140,000 homestead exemption (SB 4), grid reliability (SB 6) and water supply investment (SB 7) among his top 2025 priority bills.

Designated as 2025 priorities bills requiring local law enforcement to assist federal deportation efforts (SB 8), bail reform (SB 9 and SB 40), Ten Commandments displays in schools (SB 10), stopping non-citizen voting (SB 16) and restricting foreign adversary land purchases (SB 17).
Designated a $200,000 homestead exemption for seniors (SB 23), teacher pay increases (SB 26) and the Life of the Mother Act (SB 31) as 2025 priorities.
SB 2 (vouchers), SB 10 (Ten Commandments), SB 17 (foreign land), SB 8 (ICE agreements) and SB 9 (bail) became law in 2025; SB 3 (THC ban) was vetoed by Gov. Abbott.
Presided over the 2023 Senate impeachment trial of Attorney General Ken Paxton.
Authored the state's mandatory pre-abortion ultrasound law as a senator.
In 2020 offered a reward of up to $1 million for information on voter fraud and called expanded mail voting a scam.
Backed the 2017 bill restricting bathroom use by transgender students, which did not become law.

notes.text: Months before the Paxton trial, the Defend Texas Liberty PAC gave Patrick's campaign a $1 million contribution and a $2 million loan; Patrick had also previously donated to and loaned money to Paxton's 2018 campaign.

In September 2026 Vikki Goodwin filed a police complaint alleging two AI-generated campaign ads depicting her violated the state deepfake law; Patrick's campaign called them obvious parody, denied breaking the law and removed them the next day. No charges had been reported.
Endorsed in the 2026 primary by Donald Trump, Greg Abbott, the Combined Law Enforcement Associations of Texas, Texas Alliance for Life and Texas Gun Rights.
Reported about $24.4 million cash on hand as of Sept. 24, 2026.

q_vouchers.summary: Made school choice (SB 2) one of his top priorities; it became law in 2025.

q_school_funding.summary: Designated a teacher pay increase (SB 26) as a 2025 priority and pushed a $5,000 teacher raise in 2019.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Made SB 10, requiring Ten Commandments displays in classrooms, a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_abortion.summary: Opposes abortion exceptions for rape or incest, with an exception only when the mother's life is in danger; authored the mandatory ultrasound law.

q_border_state.summary: Lists securing the border among his priorities and says border security funding and more state troopers are funded in the budget.

q_deportation.summary: Made SB 8, requiring local law enforcement to assist federal deportation efforts, a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_gun_laws.summary: Called for closing stranger-to-stranger background check gaps in 2019, then backed expanding gun rights including permitless carry.

q_bail.summary: Made bail reform (SB 9 and SB 40) a 2025 priority, describing it as keeping violent criminals off the streets.

q_cannabis.summary: Made a ban on THC products (SB 3) a top priority and says he opposes any path to recreational marijuana.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Says he is working to strengthen the grid by adding reliable thermal power and made grid reliability (SB 6) a priority.

q_foreign_land.summary: Made SB 17, "Stopping Foreign Adversaries' Land Grabs," a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_water.summary: Made SB 7, "Increasing Investments in Texas' Water Supply," a 2025 priority; it became law.

q_voting_access.summary: Called expanded vote-by-mail a scam in 2020 and presided over the 2021 election law.

q_election_fraud.summary: Offered up to $1 million for voter fraud tips in 2020 and made stopping non-citizen voting (SB 16) a 2025 priority.

issue_notes.summary: Made raising the homestead exemption to $140,000, and to $200,000 for seniors, top 2025 priorities, along with business tax relief.
Designated bills on a parental bill of rights and limiting inappropriate books in schools as 2025 priorities.
Designated a Texas DOGE government efficiency bill as a 2025 priority.

candidates.current_role: Texas State Representative, District 47 (Travis County), since 2019; Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor
candidates.background: Vikki Goodwin runs a residential real estate business with her husband and has represented parts of Austin and the Lake Travis area in the Texas House since 2019. She grew up in Dallas and holds a business degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a master's degree from the LBJ School of Public Affairs. In the 2025 session she served on the Appropriations and Insurance committees. She won the Democratic nomination in a May 26, 2026 runoff with 67.8 percent.

priorities.text: Campaigns on well-funded neighborhood public schools and opposes vouchers.
Campaigns on protecting water and putting families ahead of data centers.
Campaigns on comprehensive, affordable health care through her Texas Cares plan.
Campaigns on affordable housing, including limiting tax increases and keeping rents down.
Says the Senate needs a leader who solicits ideas from the entire body.

promises.text: Proposes a three-tier Texas Cares plan: Medicaid expansion up to 138 percent of the poverty level, a state Basic Health Program for incomes up to 200 percent, and a state-run insurance option for all Texans.
Pledges as lieutenant governor to prioritize bills regulating data centers, making them pay for their electricity and water and giving counties power to regulate them.
Calls for a pause on new data center construction until comprehensive legislation passes.
Says she will pursue a regulatory framework for THC with age limits, testing and labeling instead of prohibition.
Supports raising the minimum wage to at least $15 an hour.

record.text: Passed Cati's Act (2023) on drowning prevention at child care facilities and the Natalia Cox Act (2023) providing resources to domestic violence victims.
Filed a 2023 bill for universal background checks and a three-day waiting period for gun purchases; it died in committee.
Voted against SB 2 (2025), the education savings account program, and for HB 2 (2025), the school finance bill.
Voted against SB 8 (2021), the six-week abortion ban, HB 1927 (2021), permitless carry, and SB 1 (2021), the election law.
Voted for SB 9 (2025), the bail bill, and SJR 5 (2025), the bail constitutional amendment.
Voted for HJR 7 (2025), the dedicated water fund amendment, and SB 7 (2025), on water infrastructure financing.
Voted for HB 441 (2021) and HB 218 (2023), reducing penalties for marijuana possession, and for HB 46 (2025), expanding the Compassionate Use Program; was recorded absent on SB 3 (2025), the THC ban.
Voted against HB 2127 (2023), the preemption law, HB 1243 (2023), the illegal voting penalty increase, and SB 2627 (2023), the electric generation funding bill.
Voted against the House versions of the 2023 and 2025 state budgets.
Took part in the 2025 quorum break over congressional redistricting and voted against HB 4 (2025), the new map.

notes.text: Attorney General Ken Paxton sought to remove Goodwin and 12 other House Democrats from office over the 2025 quorum break; the Texas Supreme Court dismissed the case in May 2026.
In September 2026 she filed a police complaint alleging that two AI-generated ads by the Patrick campaign violated the state deepfake law; the ads were removed the next day.
Endorsed by EMILYs List and by the editorial boards of the Austin American-Statesman, Houston Chronicle and San Antonio Express-News.
Says she holds an A+ rating from Equality Texas.
A poll of likely voters in late July 2026 found 56 percent of respondents did not know enough about Goodwin to have an opinion.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Supports property tax relief through the state taking greater responsibility for funding education and other services, but does not propose eliminating school property taxes.

q_min_wage.summary: Supports raising the minimum wage to at least $15 an hour and raising the tipped-worker wage.

q_vouchers.summary: Has voted against vouchers, including SB 2 (2025), and calls the program a terrible deal for Texas kids.

q_school_funding.summary: Wants to raise the basic allotment to previous levels, keep funding in line with inflation and raise teacher pay.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Voted against SB 10 (2025) and says public money should not fund religious education.

q_medicaid.summary: Proposes Medicaid expansion as the first tier of her Texas Cares plan.

q_abortion.summary: Calls for restoring full reproductive care and voted against the 2021 six-week ban.

q_border_state.summary: Supports comprehensive federal immigration reform and says Texas does not have to keep buying into the current approach; voted against SB 4 (2023).

q_deportation.summary: Criticizes what she calls ruthless and often illegal detention of people who call Texas home and voted against SB 8 (2025).

q_legal_status.summary: Supports comprehensive immigration reform and cites uncertainty for DACA students and refugees.

q_gun_laws.summary: Supports stronger background checks, training requirements and tools against straw purchases, and filed a universal background check bill in 2023.

q_bail.summary: Voted for SB 9 (2025) and SJR 5 (2025), expanding the denial of bail in certain cases.

q_cannabis.summary: Supports regulating THC rather than prohibiting it and proposes funding part of her health plan with a tax on legal cannabis.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Voted against SB 2627 (2023), which created funding mechanisms for new electric generating facilities.

q_water.summary: Voted for the 2025 water fund amendment and water financing bill, while saying conservation and reuse should be part of the answer and drinking water should come before data centers.

q_voting_access.summary: Supports online voter registration, expanded voting options and ranked choice voting in local elections.

q_election_fraud.summary: Voted against HB 1243 (2023), which increased the criminal penalty for illegal voting.

q_preemption.summary: Voted against HB 2127 (2023), which limits local ordinances.

q_gambling.summary: Favors letting Texas voters decide whether to legalize gambling.

q_trans_minors.summary: Voted against SB 14 (2023), the state ban on gender transition treatments for minors.

q_foreign_land.summary: Voted against SB 17 (2025) restricting land purchases by certain foreign entities.

issue_notes.summary: Supports a constitutional amendment allowing citizen-initiated statewide ballot measures (HJR 198).
Proposes the Fair Rent Incentive Act lowering the appraisal cap for landlords who charge fair market rent or less, and automatic homestead exemptions at closing.
Supports an employer contribution to fund child care and expanding Pre-K eligibility to children of public school employees.
Wants laws putting people and animals first for water, studies before construction and penalties for companies that do not report water use.

candidates.background: Anthony Cristo is a high school English and debate teacher and military veteran from Cibolo. He was previously the Libertarian nominee for Texas's 15th Congressional District in 2018 and the 34th District in 2020.

priorities.text: Campaigns on cutting taxes and spending, saying real tax relief requires shrinking government.
Campaigns on a balanced budget and properly funding schools without raising taxes.
Campaigns on free markets and welcoming immigrants who come to work.
Campaigns on ending the war on drugs and legalizing marijuana.

promises.text: Says he is ready to debate his opponents on the issues.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Is skeptical of property tax relief plans without spending cuts, saying shifting the burden to sales taxes is a shell game.

q_cannabis.summary: Says it is time to legalize marijuana in Texas and end prohibition.

q_deportation.summary: Supports immigrants who come to work and says politicians should stop blaming immigrants.

issue_notes.summary: Says he opposes taxpayer-funded welfare.
Says the state surplus shows Texans are taxed more than needed and that schools can be funded without tax increases.

candidates.current_role: Former high school math teacher; Green Party nominee for lieutenant governor
candidates.background: Kevin McCormick is a former high school math teacher at Jefferson High School in San Antonio who earned a law degree from the University of Houston Law Center in 1986. He has lived in San Antonio, Houston, Tyler, Longview and Carrollton and now lives near Lindale in East Texas. His campaign site also references a 2016 campaign.

priorities.text: Campaigns on serving the public interest, defined as healthy people, a healthy society and a healthy environment.
Lists investing in public transportation by expanding city bus fleets as a top legislative priority.
Lists rural investment, including family farm greenhouse cooperatives and hemp production, as a top priority.
Lists election code reform, including ranked-choice voting, a single statewide primary and limits on gerrymandering, as a top priority.
Campaigns on conserving and protecting water resources and encouraging renewable energy.

promises.text: Proposes appraising property based on rental value and household income levels instead of comparable sales, and eliminating special interest property tax exemptions.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Proposes reforming how property is appraised rather than eliminating property taxes, writing that Texans have to pay for their state.

q_vouchers.summary: Says the 2025 voucher program will further impair public education and transfers public money to the wealthy.

q_school_funding.summary: Wants to increase the number of teachers and focus resources at the classroom level.

q_medicaid.summary: Says Texas could use federal funding to expand Medicaid coverage and supports Medicare for All.

q_cannabis.summary: Says decriminalization or legalization of marijuana reduces cartel profits and does not increase crime.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Says Texas should encourage renewable energy and respond to climate change.
